1:
Delitzsch sets out what the assembly was for before the chapter says it. David meant to hand over the throne before his death, secure the succession, and make his son's great work possible, so he summoned the estates of the kingdom, the court officials and the captains to Jerusalem; there he named Solomon as divinely chosen, charged him to keep the commandments and build the house, delivered the plans, and finally gave his own treasure and called on the chiefs for a voluntary contribution. The whole chapter is a transfer of office conducted in public.

Henry reads the same occasion as a deathbed growing busier. David had served his own generation by the will of God, and now, as a type of the Son of David, the nearer he came to his end the harder he worked. Henry notes the small recovery from the illness in which they covered him with clothes and he got no heat — and asks the obvious question, what cure is there for old age — then observes that David used the recovery as an opportunity to do God and his country a little more service. He also sees why the great men had to be there: David would not settle the crown except in the presence and to the satisfaction of those who represented the people, as Moses and Joshua had gathered Israel before them.

How the old king came to be on his feet divides the witnesses four ways. Clarke has him chiefly confined to his bed, speaking to Solomon from it, and receiving strength to rise only when the nobles of the kingdom came before him. Ellicott says simply that he rose from his throne, as anyone addressing an assembly would. Delitzsch insists on the throne and rejects the alternative outright: until then David had been sitting, not lying in bed, whatever Kimchi and others inferred. Gill declines to choose, offering the couch and the throne as equal possibilities, and supports the second with a custom of the ancients by which even kings stood to address a crowd — citing the wounded Agamemnon, who would not speak sitting until he had excused himself for it. Henry, alone, has it both ways in sequence: David exerted himself to rise from his bed to give them the meeting, and then rose out of his chair to speak.

The form of address divides them again, and more sharply. Delitzsch hears in my brethren and my people a phrase expressive of condescending goodwill — a king stooping. Ellicott denies precisely that: the words imply not condescension but an acknowledgment of what every hearer already felt to be true, that all Israel were kin and David the head of the family. Henry stands nearer Ellicott, reading the king's rising itself as reverence, both toward God whose will he was about to declare and toward the assembly of the Israel of God before him.
3:
Ellicott puts the weight of the sentence on a single word. The stress falls on God, set in deliberate contrast with the I of the clause just before it — in my heart it was. The purpose had been David's own; the refusal was not, and the grammar marks the change of speaker. Gill supplies the channel by which the refusal arrived: it was said to David by Nathan the prophet, not heard directly by the king himself.

Delitzsch fills in what was being refused. The house of rest was to be for the ark of the covenant and for the footstool of the feet of our God, which is to say for the ark and for the covering upon it; that covering is called the footstool because God was enthroned above the cherubim there. And the phrase rendered had made ready for the building means what it says in the plainest sense, that labour and materials had already been laid in. Delitzsch also observes that almost nothing here is new. In substance David had said all of it once before, privately, to his son; what the assembly hears is that private charge repeated in public and on the record.

The chain of election is traced downward, and the commentators press on its links. Gill notes that the choice of David passed over every one of his elder brothers. Ellicott presses on the wording twice. He hath chosen Judah to be the ruler is better read as For Judah it was that he chose for prince, and then, within the house of Judah, my father's house. And he liked me he calls scarcely adequate: the Hebrew verb answers to the Greek for being well pleased or satisfied, so the line should run, It was I in whom He took pleasure. Ellicott then makes the observation that gives the phrase its reach — David uses of himself the very words the voice from heaven spoke of the Son of David at his baptism.

Over how far for ever reaches, the witnesses part. Gill takes it by stages: a long time, as long as David lived; or rather in his posterity for many years to come; and best of all in his antitype. Clarke makes the stages a condition instead. The government should have had no end, provided they continued to walk according to the commandments — the proviso David himself attaches two verses later — but as the promise refers to Christ it is and will be without end.

Ellicott closes on the throne of the kingdom of the Lord, an expression he calls unique in the Old Testament. It throws into strong relief the idea that the Israelite monarchy was only a vicegerency: neither David nor Solomon but the Lord was the true and only King, which was Gideon's reason for refusing the crown when it was offered him.
6:
Ellicott hears an emphasis in the Hebrew that the English flattens. He shall build my house is better rendered he it is that shall build: the pronoun is emphatic, and its force is he, and not thou. What David is repeating to the assembly is not merely a commission given to Solomon but the sentence that excluded David himself, stated from the other side. Ellicott renders the adoption clause just as literally — I have chosen him for myself as a son, and I, I will become to him a father — where the doubled pronoun does the same work a second time.

Wesley takes that sonship forward. A son chosen, a house to be built, a father promised: so was Solomon a figure of him that was to come, who is both the founder and the foundation of the gospel temple. The builder of the second house is himself the stone the second house is built on, which is more than Solomon could be said to be of the first.

The condition attached to the promise draws the closest reading. Ellicott notes that the identical proviso is attached to the identical promise in the parallel history of the kings, where the offer of length of days carries it too. As at this day he glosses as we are doing in our present work — the same words, he adds, occur in the same sense at the close of Solomon's own prayer of dedication. Wesley reads the phrase as he hath begun, pointing not at the assembly's present labour but at the young king's own start. Where Wesley goes further than Ellicott is in dividing the promise itself: it is absolute with regard to the Messiah, but conditional with regard to Solomon; and the application follows at once, that if we are constant in our duty, then and not otherwise, we may expect the continuance of his favour.

The charge to the people is put as a legal appeal. Ellicott gives the literal shape — And now to the eyes of all Israel, and in the ears of our God — and supplies the verb the Hebrew leaves out, I adjure you. He compares it to the solemn appeal Moses made in calling heaven and earth to witness; here the witnesses are the whole nation as represented before the king, and the God whose ear is ever open. Clarke records what the Targum did with the same clause, reading in the audience of our God as Before the Word of the Lord.

On what David asks of them the two teachers differ in scope. Ellicott makes seek mean do not neglect: resort to the commandments always, as the rule of right living. Wesley splits the pair of verbs and gets a program of study out of it — keep those commands which you know, and search into what you are yet ignorant of, that you may distinctly understand the whole will of God. His warning is that they cannot be kept without great care.

What hangs on it is territorial. Ellicott hears in the promise of this good land and the inheritance left to children yet another echo of the farewell discourses of Moses, where possession is always bound to fidelity. Wesley sharpens the threat implicit in the summons: David calls upon God, present among them, and upon the whole nation gathered there by its representatives, to testify against any man who disregards his counsel.
9:
Gill marks the pivot. Solomon was present in the assembly and had just been presented to it as successor and future king; having finished with the estates, David turns from them and speaks to his son directly, in their hearing. Ellicott describes the turn the same way and names its burden: a whole-hearted service owed to his father's God.

Whose God that is gets a careful answer. Ellicott allows that the God of thy father could mean simply the God of Israel, but prefers the narrower sense, the God of David, and takes his reason from later in this same speech, where the old king says my God without qualification. The verb governing it is drawn out rather than translated: know thou is regard thou, have care for. Wesley reaches the same practical place by a different route, observing that words of knowledge in scripture commonly imply affection and practice, so that to know is to love and serve, or else to acknowledge him as thy God by loving and obeying him.

The two demands are then weighed word by word. Ellicott notes that the term behind a perfect heart means whole, sound, unimpaired — the Latin integer — so that what is urged is undivided allegiance rather than moral flawlessness. And a willing mind is not decoration: service is not real unless it be voluntary, and so glad as well as free. Ellicott also catches a link the English hides, that the verb rendered searcheth is the same one rendered seek a verse earlier; the Searcher of hearts will at once see through an insincere and half-hearted obedience. What he discerns is every fashioning or cast of thoughts, not only the finished ones. Wesley turns that on Solomon personally: if thou dost only put on a profession of religion to please me, thou mayest indeed deceive me, but thou canst not deceive him.

On the threat the two are unusually blunt. Ellicott insists that forsake means deliberately and of set purpose, as choosing to live by other laws than his, and that cast thee off translates a strong word meaning strictly to reject as noisome or foul-smelling — a verbal form peculiar to this book. He balances it on the other side: seeking in earnest always results in finding, and the divine grace is not even restricted by that condition. Wesley measures the threat by what it would cancel, namely all the promises made to David and to his seed, and the great honour and favour already shewn to Solomon himself.

Take heed now is read two ways. Gill offers both without choosing: take heed of offending God by forsaking him, or else see, consider, and observe what David is about to say next. Ellicott takes it as introducing a fact rather than a warning — See now that the Lord hath chosen thee, weigh this high commission and realise it thoroughly, then be strong and act. Wesley adds only the courage clause: without it we can do no work of God as we ought.
11:
Both of the close readers notice that the list has a direction. Ellicott says the description proceeds from the outer to the inner; Delitzsch maps the same movement over three verses — first the temple house, working from outside in, then the courts and the buildings standing in them, then the vessels. The word rendered pattern is the same one used of the model of the tabernacle shown to Moses; neither commentator presses the parallel, but neither lets it pass.

The rooms themselves are harder to fix, and here Ellicott and Wesley disagree. Ellicott takes the houses thereof to mean the temple's two principal rooms, the holy place and the holy of holies, or as he puts it, the nave and the chancel; the inner parlours he then identifies as the vestibule and the nave, set in contrast with the place of the mercy seat, the inmost shrine. Wesley agrees about the houses but not about the parlours: for him these are the rooms built against the wall of the house round about, the side chambers rather than any part of the main hall. On the last item Wesley is content to say only that the phrase fixes in what particular part of the holy of holies the mercy seat was to stand.

One word in the verse occurs nowhere else, and the commentators go at it from opposite ends. Clarke reports that the term is not Hebrew at all but supposed Persian, where the related word means a granary, a hidden treasure, a barn; and he passes on Parkhurst's guess that it is compounded of a verb meaning to treasure up and an adjective meaning pure, so that the sense would be a treasury for the most precious things. Ellicott collects the same Persian evidence, but then cites Gesenius for the opposite conclusion: the root passed from the Semitic tongues into Persian, not the other way. He also does the arithmetic on the upper chambers, which he places over the holy of holies: its ceiling stood twenty cubits from the floor and the roof thirty from the ground, leaving a space ten cubits high by twenty each way.

Whether the next verse begins a new list is itself disputed. The old versions, and the Authorised translation after them, read it as a written description of the courses of the priests and Levites handed over with the plans. Ellicott admits the Hebrew allows that but prefers to hook the words back to the chambers round about: the cells were for the priests and Levites to lodge in by course, not merely for stowage. Delitzsch reads it the same way and itemises the work done there — baking the shewbread, cooking the sacrificial flesh, holding the sacrificial meals, housing the vessels used for all of it. Ellicott adds a Syriac paraphrase that supplies the same detail from another direction, naming among the temple buildings a house of the water-carriers and a house of the lampmen.

How the plan reached David is the last question. Clarke calls what was handed over a full architectural set, with elevations, sections and specifications of every part, all of it received by inspiration. Gill and Clarke both cite the Targum, which makes it the spirit of prophecy that was with him, and Gill records a Jewish tradition that Samuel was let into the design first and passed it on. Henry and Wesley both think it was given in writing, probably by the ministry of an angel, or else impressed on his mind as clearly as if it had been written. Henry states the reason bluntly: the contrivance of David's devotion or of Solomon's wisdom must not be trusted in a matter of this nature, since the house was a kind of sacrament and could not be left to man's art or invention.
14:
What David handed over in these verses was not bullion but an inventory. Ellicott, noting how concise the Hebrew is, reconstructs the sense at length: he gave him a pattern or description for the golden vessels, by the weight, for all vessels of each kind of use, and likewise for all the silver ones. In plainer words, David gave Solomon a schedule of every vessel the sanctuary would require, with the exact weight of each specified against it. Clarke says the same thing in a line — the quantity of gold which was to be put in each article — and Gill adds the claim that governs the whole list, that David was directed by the Spirit of God what weight or quantity was to go into each thing made.

The lampstands show how far the new house had outgrown the old. Clarke states the contrast baldly: there was but one chandelier in the tabernacle, and there were ten in the temple. Gill has the same ten and goes further, reporting the Jewish arrangement by which they stood five on one side of the older Mosaic lampstand and five on the other, and citing an authority who puts the gold for each at a hundred pounds. Ellicott, who renders the clause carefully as a specified weight for each lampstand and its lamps, stops at a detail the others pass over: the silver lampstands mentioned here are named nowhere else in the whole Old Testament. What became of them he can report only from the rabbis, who place them in the chambers of the priests.

The closing phrase of that verse divides Ellicott from Wesley. Ellicott takes according to the use of every candlestick as a measurement clause, meaning according to the service each lampstand was to perform. Wesley hears a distinction of another kind altogether, between lampstands fixed in one place — of which he counts ten in the holy place — and lampstands meant to be carried from place to place.

The tables raise a harder problem, because the older law knows only one table of shewbread and this verse has several. Gill resolves it by counting: one in the tabernacle of Moses, ten in the temple of Solomon, each of a hundred pounds. Wesley resolves it by rank, allowing that there were divers tables used about the shewbread while one of them was of more eminency than the rest, and so is commonly called the table of the shewbread in the singular. Ellicott resolves it by text. He points out that the chronicler plainly knew there had been only one, since he says so elsewhere, and that the ten golden tables Solomon made, set five on the right and five on the left, may be what is meant here. Then he floats a conjecture the others do not attempt: that the word shewbread is a gloss which has pushed out the word gold, and that the original read for the tables of gold — which would match the tables of silver at the end of the same verse and quietly fold the one shewbread table in among the rest. On those silver tables Ellicott can again say only that the Old Testament never mentions them again, and that the rabbis put them in the court, for the prepared flesh of the sacrificial victims to be laid upon.
17:
The last of the vessels are small and domestic, and the commentators keep them so. Gill explains the fleshhooks by their use, to take the pieces of flesh out of the pots in which they were boiled. Ellicott would rather call them forks, and renders the whole clause as an inventory entry: the forks, the bowls and the flagons were pure gold. He assigns each its office — the bowls for lustral sprinkling, the golden flagons for libations — and identifies the golden basons as tankards or lidded pitchers, a word found only here and in the list of sacred vessels Cyrus gave back.

One item is singled out as purer than the rest, and Wesley will not let the detail lie flat. The refined gold of the altar of incense was purer than any of the other gold in the house, and it was typical of the intercession of Christ, than which nothing can be more pure and perfect.

Then comes the chariot, and here the witnesses genuinely part company. Ellicott and Delitzsch agree on what the word means: the two figures resting on the covering of the ark are themselves called the chariot, because God is said to ride upon a cherub, and Delitzsch insists the grammar bears this out — the cherubim stand in explanatory apposition to the chariot, not in the genitive under it. It is the cherubim, not the ark, that form the chariot on which God is enthroned. Wesley dissents outright on which cherubim are meant. These, he says, are not the pair fastened to the mercy seat, for Moses had made those long before; they are the far larger figures Solomon was still to make, whose wings reached from wall to wall. And Wesley reads the verb accordingly: they covered the ark not above it, since Moses's cherubim already did that, but before it, screening it from the eyes of the high priest when he entered the most holy place. Clarke supplies the Targum, which flattens the difficulty by making the chariot merely like in figure to the propitiatory where the golden cherubim spread their wings. Wesley alone draws a moral from the word chariot itself: since a chariot is made to carry a person from place to place, the term may hint that God was not so fixed to the new house that he would not remove from it if they forsook him.

How the plan came is left genuinely open. Gill lists the options without hiding his preference — an impulse of the Spirit that left the design as clear as if written, or the Jewish tradition that Samuel or some other prophet received it first and passed it to David in writing, or, as Gill himself sees no reason to deny, a handwriting from the Lord delivered by angels, as the two tables were. Wesley offers the same alternatives more briefly, a man of God who wrote it down, or a writing made by God's own hand upon the table of David's mind. Clarke prefers a vision of ecstasy in which a fully sketched plan was impressed so deeply that David could describe it afterwards, and he quotes Delaney for the claim that Greek architecture descends from this design as from its fountain. Ellicott and Delitzsch both worry at the grammar instead. Ellicott cannot decide whether the writing came by the hand of one of David's seers or was simply the older description of the Mosaic sanctuary, notes that the verb wants an object the Hebrew does not supply, and ends by suspecting the text is corrupt. Delitzsch, weighing where the phrase upon me attaches, settles on the writing rather than the hand, so that the sense is what is prescribed to me.
20:
Ellicott sets the closing words back in their place: this is the conclusion of the charge David began before he broke off to hand over the plans, and the long transfer of designs and weights was an interruption in the middle of a speech. He notices too that the encouragement given earlier has picked up an extra verb. Be strong and of good courage stood alone when David said it in private; here and do it is added, because the time for action is now imminent.

The promise attached to it is quoted rather than composed. Delitzsch and Ellicott both trace it to the assurance given when Moses handed his own work to a successor and repeated to Joshua — he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee. Ellicott presses on the verb: to fail is to drop, to let go, and so to dismiss or desert. He is equally careful with the limit. When David says until thou hast finished all the work, the word implies nothing whatever about the time beyond the stated point; it marks the end of the guarantee, not the end of the help.

On the two words my God the witnesses converge. Delitzsch, borrowing a phrase from an older commentator, says David uses the possessive to call to mind how often he had been preserved in many dangers. Wesley expands the same thought into speech David does not quite make: whom I have chosen and served, who has all along been with me and prospered me, I recommend thee to him. Wesley then draws the line most often quoted from this chapter: God never leaves any, unless they first leave him. Clarke records how the Targum renders the clause, making not God himself but the Word of the Lord Solomon's assistant.

Whether the priests and Levites were standing in front of David as he spoke is a real disagreement, and it turns on a single particle. Ellicott takes the form of expression to suggest that David pointed to them; the representatives of religion would hardly be missing from an assembly of all the princes of Israel. He reads the following clause the same way, as another gesture toward the princes and all the people. Delitzsch will not grant it. The behold refers to the priests and Levites as divided into their classes, and that reference does not presuppose their presence in the assembly at all — it points at an institution, not at a group of men in the room. Gill supplies what makes the reference intelligible either way: these were the courses David had lately fixed, to take their turns in the temple once it was built.

The help promised is of three kinds, and Clarke gathers them in one breath — the priests and the Levites, the cunning artificers, and the princes of the people will be at thy command. Ellicott adds what the Hebrew makes of those artificers: the word behind willing skilful man strictly means one who brings a free-will offering, so that the sense is every volunteer with skill, in every kind of work. The phrase volunteer with wisdom, he observes, is found nowhere else. Delitzsch stops over a small particle in the same clause which Bertheau wanted to delete as a copying error; Delitzsch keeps it, on the ground that this book uses the form often and that it serves to bring the subject into emphatic prominence. The last phrase, wholly at thy commandment, Ellicott renders literally as for all thy words — that is, thy orders, or simply thy business. Clarke closes on the father rather than the son, finding piety, good sense, prudence and zeal for the public welfare all united in one old man, who set before Solomon his danger, his duty and his interest in the truest and most impressive light.
